   topics, in order: `settingsd.desktop.changed.<profile>` (schema 1),
   `settingsd.desktop.compact.<profile>` (schema 2), then the summary. A
   revision is published once all three are; a failure retries all three.
   noded reserves the compact topic for settingsd as it does the others.
4. **Ported consumers move now.** The shared native consumer
   (`settings::native`) follows the compact topic and reads schema 2, and
   the portal asks for schema 2. Measured with the embedded design, the
   compact snapshot is about 72 KB where schema 1 is 499 KB.
5. **Unported consumers move with their port.** An application or service
   still on its own copy of the settings library keeps following the schema
   1 topic and reading schema 1. Each moves when it is ported, by using the
   shared consumer. Nothing in an unported consumer changes for this
   decision.

## Retiring schema 1

The schema 1 topic and default stay while any consumer still uses them.
Publishing schema 1 costs a full snapshot per change, so once the last
consumer has moved, a later decision stops publishing it and makes schema 2
the default read. The library keeps decoding schema 1 for caches and old
retained state.

## Not chosen

Deltas between revisions, compression and local compilation are discussed
in the summary decision. Schema 2 removes duplication without changing what
a consumer holds; local compilation (no projection on the wire) remains the
next step once consumers can pin the design source by digest.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-summary-reads/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-11-settings-summary-reads.md) -->

# Plain settings followers read a summary, not the snapshot

Status: accepted. Settings contract 0.2.0 (additive). Builds on
[Desktop settings have one native ABP authority](2026-10-07-settings-authority.md).

## Context

The settings snapshot carries the profile's complete effective design: one
compiled projection per context (the desktop and each native app). Measured
on a running session with the embedded design source:

- a `settings.get` reply is 499 KB of JSON, 498 KB of it `effective`: seven
  byte-identical 71 KB projections, 62 KB of each a button table;
- settingsd publishes that whole snapshot as the retained payload of
  `settingsd.desktop.changed.<profile>`;
- an application following the session look on a plain Bus connection
  (`settings::follow::Follower`) cannot verify a delivery's publisher, so it
  treats the delivery as a hint and reads `settings.get` again. It uses only
  the profile's identity, revision and appearance names.

One appearance change therefore moved about 0.5 MB to every plain follower
twice (the delivery and the re-read), and each parsed it. Idle traffic is
zero; the cost is per change. Native consumers (the portal, the compositor's
scene host and applications using the shared `settings` consumer) do use the
projections, from owner-stamped deliveries.

## Decision

1. **A summary topic.** settingsd also publishes a retained
   `settingsd.desktop.summary.<profile>` whose payload is a
   `settings::Summary`: schema, binding, incarnation, revision, design
   revision, source digest, the appearance names and `custom_source`. It
   never carries the projections or a custom design source. noded reserves
   it for settingsd exactly as it reserves the snapshot topic: only the
   registered `settingsd` service may publish or clear it, and inner routing
   headers are canonicalised. A revision counts as published once both
   topics are; a failure retries both.
2. **A summary read.** `settings.get` takes an optional `view`: `full` (the
   default, the complete snapshot as before) or `summary` (the same
   `Summary` under `summary`, with the usual status fields). An unknown view
   is refused like any unknown field. A request without `view` reads exactly
   as it did under 0.1.0, and the field is never sent at its default.
3. **Plain followers move to the summary.** The `Follower` subscribes to
   the summary topic and reads the summary view; Prefs does the same. A
   follower still treats a delivery only as a hint: this decision does not
   change how deliveries are trusted.
4. **Native consumers are unchanged.** The snapshot topic and the full view
   keep their schema and behaviour for every consumer that uses projections.

Measured on the same session after the change, one appearance change sends
a plain follower a 566-byte summary delivery and a 587-byte summary read,
where it had a 542 KB delivery and a 542 KB read. The remaining large
transfers belong to native consumers: the snapshot publish, the portal's
`settings.appearance.get` and the compositor scene host's full read, each
about 542 KB. They are the subject of the deduplication step below.

## Rollout

The summary topic is new, so the order matters: noded (the reservation),
then settingsd (publishes and serves the summary), then the followers. A
follower that reaches a settingsd without the summary view is refused
(`unknown field`) and keeps its last look, and it hears no hints from a
settingsd that does not publish the summary topic. Roll back in the reverse
order.

## Considered and deferred

- **Deduplicating `effective` by content digest** (one copy per distinct
  projection, contexts naming a digest) would make the full snapshot about
  72 KB. It changes snapshot schema 1, which native consumers decode and the
  optional cache stores, so it needs a schema 2 negotiated per request and
  the consumer, reducer and cache moving together. It is the next step for
  native consumers.
- **Compiling projections locally from the summary.** A projection is a
  function of the pinned source and the selected axes, and native consumers
  already link the design library: they could compile instead of
  transferring, at a few milliseconds per context. It needs the source
  pinned by digest and a compiler-version check, which the cache already
  records.
- **Immutable artifacts fetched by digest** remain the planned path for
  settings too large to inline (the 960 KiB snapshot ceiling).
- **Deltas between revisions** are not worth it: a scheme change rewrites
  most colour values in a projection, so a JSON delta is nearly the size of
  the projection. A summary is already smaller than any delta of it.
- **Compression** under the frozen ABP framing would mean base64 bodies;
  WebSocket permessage-deflate is not available in the Bus's WebSocket
  library and its window is too small for repeated 71 KB projections.
- **Trusting summary deliveries** (dropping the re-read) needs the
  publisher stamp noded already records to reach plain clients. It is a
  separate change to the Bus client API.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-11-verb-classes/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-11-verb-classes.md) -->

# Decision — verb classes

Status: accepted 2026-10-11. Amends AGENTS.md §5 (Bus verbs are wire
contracts).

## The decision

- **The verb registry moves to schema 2.** Every entry in
  `docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix` gains a `class`, one of:

  | class | Meaning | Examples |
  |---|---|---|
  | `intent` | Changes what an application or service holds, or what another caller would see, at someone's request | `<app>.open`, `<app>.execute`, `<app>.refresh`, `settings.apply`, `releases.notes` (it fetches when nothing is cached), `<app>.quit`, `<app>.window` |
  | `query` | Changes nothing another caller could observe. The one allowance: it may write the artefact it was asked for and returns, such as a screenshot | `<app>.ping`, `.info`, `.state`, `.commands`, `.ui.tree`, `.ui.capture`, `.window.state`, `settings.get`, `ced.wait` |
  | `input` | Synthetic low-level input, standing in for a person's hands | `<app>.ui.click`, `.ui.pointer`, `.ui.scroll`, `.ui.key`, `.ui.type` |
  | `system` | Session plumbing. The single-instance activation verb `<app>.show` is `system` even when something calls it directly | `<app>.show` |

- **The class describes the verb, not one call.** A verb that both reads and
  changes state is `intent`.
- **When in doubt, it is `intent`.** Dropping a real action is worse than
  keeping a read.
- **A verb an application describes as `read_only` is a `query`.** Each
  application's registry test checks this. The reverse need not hold:
  `.ui.capture` writes a file, so it is not read-only, but it is still a
  query.
- **The registry gate** (`tools/verb_registry.mix`) refuses:
  - a schema other than 2;
  - an entry that is not in the canonical one-line form;
  - an unknown or missing field;
  - a bad name, owner, status or version;
  - a duplicate;
  - a class outside the four.

## Why

Tools that watch the Bus need to know what a verb is for:

- a recorder keeps intent and drops reads;
- a live traffic view colours them differently;
- an agent asked "what changed?" looks only at intent.

Without a declared class, each tool guesses from verb names, and the guesses
drift apart. The registry already declares every verb's owner, version and
status, so its purpose belongs there too.

## Consequences

- Every existing entry is classified in one change, together with the gate.
- A new verb is registered with its class from its first commit.
- Classes are about purpose, not replay. A recorder still needs each owner's
  replay rules ([rec and play](2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md)), for example
  that `ced.wait` is a deliberate ordering point.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-hostd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-hostd.md) -->

# Decision — hostd, the host service

Status: accepted 2026-10-12.

## The decision

- **One service, `hostd`, runs as root on each host.** It has two jobs:
  information about the host (hardware, OS, the MixOS mode, network
  management state, devices, power) and privileged actions on the host.
  It is the host agent of the VT-native design: the only MixOS code on the
  host besides `mix`.
- **No generic exec.** No verb runs a caller-supplied command, script or
  shell string. Each verb does one job, checks its arguments against a
  schema and does the work natively (writes the file itself, calls
  networkd, resolved, logind or iwd over Varlink or D-Bus).
- **Written in Rust.** Mix is the client. A root process that interprets
  scripts is too much attack surface.
- **A verb that can't be reversed is not added.**
- **Every new verb is reviewed on its own,** and the verb list stays short.

### Callers and transport

- **Local callers** use a Unix socket. Identity comes from the kernel
  (`SO_PEERCRED`) and the caller's cgroup, never from the request.
- **Reads are also served on the Bus,** like any other service's.
- **Writes from other nodes** are accepted only when signed by a controller
  key listed in that host's policy, over the target node, a nonce and an
  expiry. Mesh trust alone never authorises a write. A host with no listed
  controller accepts no remote writes. Enforcement is on the receiving
  host.
- **Ports below 1024 are not hostd's job.** A service that binds one gets
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` in its own unit.

### Tiers

| Tier | Examples | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| read | host info, network state, devices | caller identity |
| reversible | Wi-Fi connect, link configuration, device bind, suspend | a standing grant, plus a dead-man check or a kept previous state |
| reversible, wide blast radius | firewall, host package upgrade, reboot | a grant, a second signature from an independent reviewer, and a rate limit |
| irreversible | — | no verb exists |

### Autonomy within limits set in advance

- **Standing grants,** not per-call prompts. A grant names the caller (from
  the kernel), the verbs, argument limits and an optional expiry. Only
  creating or widening a grant needs a person, confirmed through physical
  input that no Bus caller can synthesise.
- **Reversible by construction.** A verb applies its change, runs a health
  check, and reverts unless the check passes in time. It keeps the previous
  state (the previous file, or a filesystem snapshot) behind a receipt that
  `hostd.undo` restores.
- **Limits:** a rate limit per caller and verb, a circuit breaker after
  repeated rollbacks, and a `freeze` that drops hostd to reads only.
- **Audit:** one journal record per call.

### Files hostd owns

hostd writes only files it names itself (networkd files are
`/etc/systemd/network/50-hostd-*`) and never edits a file it didn't write.

## Why

- Agents need to change host configuration (network, WireGuard, power,
  devices) without `sudo` from a session, and without a person approving
  each call.
- MixOS core has no polkit. hostd is the mechanism and its policy in one
  small binary, with rules as data instead of scripts.
- Closed verbs make a stolen credential worth far less than a root shell.

## Consequences

- Session code never shells out to `sudo`; a missing host action is a new
  hostd verb.
- Write verbs arrive one reviewed verb at a time. The first is
  `net.link.apply`; the verbs, grants and refusals are documented in the
  [host service manual](../hostd.md).
- **Root on the host** means uid 0 in hostd's own pid and user namespaces,
  proven through a pidfd. Root inside a container is never root on the
  host, with or without uid remapping.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-non-root-install-and-service-ports/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-non-root-install-and-service-ports.md) -->

# Decision — non-root install, per-service users, mesh-first ports

Status: proposed 2026-10-12. Builds on
[one repository, install profiles](2026-10-12-one-repository-install-profiles.md)
and the one-system-binary design (every headless daemon a personality of
`mix`, chosen by `argv[0]`), which needs its own decision record.

## The question

The server programs (maild, webd, dnsd and the rest) are moving into MixOS,
headed for one `mix` binary. Updates already reach desktop users through
releasesd, which by rule never changes anything as root. Can a whole node,
servers included, be installed and kept current without root, and how do
unprivileged daemons serve ports 25, 53, 443, 465, 587 and 993?

## Where these servers run

The usual MixOS server is a node on its owner's own WireGuard mesh, a /24
of their machines. Mail, web and DNS are served to that mesh, not to the
internet. A server that must take connections from outside the mesh (an MX
on public port 25, a public website on 443) is the exception. This record
covers the mesh case and states what it does not settle for the public one.

## The decision

### 1. Root installs once; updates never need it

- **Bootstrap (root, once per node, and again only when units change):**
  create the system users, install the unit, socket, sysusers and tmpfiles
  files, and hand the server prefix to the `mixos` user.
- **The server prefix `/opt/mixos` is owned by the system user `mixos`.**
  A releasesd instance running as `mixos` keeps it current, with the same
  checks as a desktop install (GitHub digest and `SHA256SUMS`, staged
  unpack, previous version kept for rollback). It uses releasesd's existing
  layout through its environment: `MIXOS_RELEASES_ROOT=/opt/mixos`, so
  releases land in `/opt/mixos/opt/<app>/<version>` and their programs are
  linked into `/opt/mixos/bin`. The unit paths (`/opt/mixos/bin/<daemon>`)
  do not change.
- **Desktop installs stay per user** in `~/.local`, as today.
- Binaries are readable and executable by everyone and writable only by
  `mixos`. No daemon runs as `mixos`.

### 2. Every daemon runs as its own user

- Each server daemon runs as its own system user (`maild`, `webd`, `dnsd`
  and so on), declared in its component's sysusers fragment. Never as root,
  never as a login user, never as `mixos`.
- Each daemon's state lives in its own `StateDirectory=`, which no other
  service user can read. A compromised webd cannot read mail, keys or the
  login user's home.
- Units use systemd's sandboxing (`NoNewPrivileges=yes`,
  `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=yes`, `PrivateTmp=yes` and a
  `CapabilityBoundingSet=` that names only what the daemon needs), and each
  component's units are reviewed against that list.

### 3. Privileged ports come from systemd

- **Socket activation is the target.** A system `.socket` unit binds the
  privileged ports as root and passes the open sockets to the daemon
  (`LISTEN_FDS`). The daemon never holds a capability. Socket activation
  also keeps the listening socket open across a restart, so an upgrade
  drops no connections that are still queued.
- **Interim:** a daemon that cannot take inherited sockets yet gets
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` with
  `CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` in its unit. Taking
  inherited sockets is part of each port's definition of done (maild,
  webd, dnsd).
- **Not file capabilities.** The kernel clears them whenever the file is
  replaced, so every update would silently lose the ports. In the one
  binary they would also give the `mix` shell, and every script, the right
  to bind 443.
- **Not lowering `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` by default.** It
  applies to every user on the node. A node owner may still choose it for a
  single-user machine, but MixOS does not do it for them.

### 4. Mesh first

- Server daemons listen on the node's mesh address by default, never on
  every address. The `.socket` units name the mesh address
  (`ListenStream=<mesh-ip>:25`, with `FreeBind=yes` so the socket can be
  bound before the WireGuard interface is up).
- Listening on a public address is an explicit per-node configuration,
  never a default and never part of an install profile.

### 5. Applying an update without root

- releasesd (as `mixos`) moves `current` and records the transition in
  `meta.json`. A root-owned systemd `.path` unit watches that file and
  starts a root service that restarts only the units whose component
  version or hash changed in the release manifest. The `mixos` user
  triggers the restart but never controls which units restart or how.
- A release whose units, sysusers or tmpfiles fragments changed cannot be
  applied by `mixos`. releasesd installs the binaries, reports that the
  bootstrap step is needed, and leaves the running services on the
  previous version until a root user runs the installer.

### 6. What still needs root at run time

- **nspawnd:** `systemd-nspawn` needs root. It stays a root service in its
  own profile, outside this model.
- **noded:** reading network state needs nothing; changing it needs
  `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, granted in its unit the same way as the interim port
  capability, only if that node uses the feature.
- **compd:** none. Seat, input and display access come through logind and
  libseat, as today.

## Not settled: servers open to the internet

A daemon that accepts connections from outside the mesh (an MX on public
port 25, a public website on 443) faces hostile traffic. Running it as its
own sandboxed user, with the port granted by systemd, is still the baseline.
It is not shown to be enough: rate limits, DoS behaviour, TLS and ACME
exposure, whether the public listener should be its own process or node, and
firewall policy all belong to a separate decision before any public
listener ships as a supported configuration.

## Why

- **Updates without root** are what make the releasesd model work for a
  whole operating system: no package manager, no distribution repository,
  and no root shell for routine updates.
- **Per-service users** limit what one compromised daemon can reach. Running
  every daemon as the login user would have been simpler, but would have
  handed a mail-server bug the owner's SSH keys and secrets.
- **Ports from systemd** grant the right per service and per port, survive
  updates, and keep capabilities away from the shell that shares the
  binary.
- **Mesh first** matches how MixOS servers are used, and keeps the
  internet-facing case visible as the exception it is.

## Alternatives

- **Everything as the login user** (user units with lingering, plus the
  sysctl). Rejected: no isolation between daemons or from the owner's home.
- **File capabilities on `mix`.** Rejected: lost on every update, and
  granted to every script.
- **Root installs through a package manager.** Rejected: it is the
  dependency that releasesd removes.
- **Root-run releasesd for the server prefix.** Rejected: releasesd's trust
  rule (never act as root) is what makes a bad release unable to take over
  the node. A fixed `.path` unit for restarts keeps root's part small.

## Consequences

- Each server component ships a sysusers fragment, its units with the
  sandboxing list, and `.socket` units for its ports. The install-profile
  resolver lists them, as that decision already requires.
- maild, webd and dnsd learn to take inherited sockets as part of their
  ports.
- releasesd gains a server instance (`mixos` user, `/opt/mixos` root) and a
  "units changed" result. The restart service and its `.path` unit are new
  work, alongside the installer the install-profiles decision calls for.
- The bootstrap installer is the only routine root step, and it runs again
  only when a release changes units.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-one-repository-install-profiles/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-one-repository-install-profiles.md) -->

# Decision — one repository, install profiles

Status: accepted 2026-10-12; amended 2026-10-12 after review. AGENTS.md
§2.3 (identity and metadata), §2.5 (Mix components) and §10 (the
checklist) are amended in the same change that adds the `profiles` field
and its gate.

## The question

MixOS has two audiences: a desktop (the compositor, the apps and their
settings services) and servers (mail, web, blobs, DNS and the mesh daemons
on headless nodes). The server programs have not moved into this
repository yet. Should they get a repository of their own?

## The decision

- **Everything stays in this repository and its one Cargo workspace.**
  Desktop, server, command-line and library code alike. There is no second
  MixOS source repository for server programs.
- **The split is an install split, not a source split.** Every shipping
  component declares the **install profiles** that include it:

  | Profile | Meaning |
  |---|---|
  | `base` | On every MixOS system: the shell and the Bus node |
  | `server` | What a headless node may run |
  | `desktop` | The desktop session: compositor, apps, their services and the session's own wiring |

- **Composition.** `server` and `desktop` each include `base`: resolving
  either one yields its own components plus `base`'s. A system may install
  both. A resolved set is the union of its profiles, each component once.
- **Who declares.** A component's *principal* package declares `profiles`:
  the package whose name is its component (the directory under `apps/`,
  `services/` or `cli/`), or a Mix component's `component.mx`. The list is
  non-empty, has no duplicates and names only the three profiles. The field
  is absent on libraries, on a component's private crates (whatever `kind`
  they inherit from their owner), and on `tool` and `test` packages.
  Libraries are never installed on their own; they are linked into what
  needs them. The session's targets and wiring (`session/`) belong to
  `desktop`; when the `session` kind lands, it declares `profiles` like any
  other shipping component.
- **Where it is declared.** A Rust component adds `profiles` to its
  `[package.metadata.mixos]`:

  ```toml
  [package.metadata.mixos]
  component = "webd"
  kind = "service"
  layer = "core"
  contract = "public"
  profiles = ["server"]
  ```

  A Mix component adds the same `profiles` list to its `component.mx`.
- **Naming.** Install profiles are unrelated to Cargo's build profiles
  (`release`, `release-fast`) and to any service's own settings profiles.
  Prose says "install profile"; tools take `--install-profile`, beside
  `--cargo-profile` and `--target`, never a bare `--profile`.
- **The profile gate** is new, workspace-wide work. Today's closure and
  layering gates check compd's own crates only; they do not protect other
  components. The profile gate:
  - refuses the declaration errors above;
  - refuses a `base` or `server` component that itself declares the
    `desktop` layer;
  - resolves the normal and build dependency closure of each `base` and
    `server` principal, for every feature set its profiles build, and
    refuses any `desktop`-layer workspace package in it, and any upstream
    GUI crate (smithay, egui, eframe, wgpu, winit, Bevy and the like) even
    though those carry no MixOS metadata;
  - for a Mix component, which has no Cargo closure, refuses a `desktop`
    layer in a `base` or `server` component; what it calls on the Bus is
    checked at review, as AGENTS.md §2.5 already says.

  The component index (`docs/dev/components.md`) shows each component's
  profiles.
- **Resolving, installing and activating are separate.**
  - **Resolve:** one tool answers "what is in `server`?" from the metadata,
    deterministically. Its output covers the packages to build, the Mix
    components, and each component's runtime artefacts: units by class
    (system or session), `sysusers` and `tmpfiles` fragments, and assets.
    Build scripts, images and installers never keep their own lists.
  - **Install:** places those files. Rust components go to an installer
    that gives binaries and units the record, rollback and drift check
    `tools/component_install.mix` gives Mix components (separate work that
    follows this decision); Mix components go to that existing installer.
  - **Activate:** which services a particular node runs, with what
    configuration, is that node's decision, not the profile's. Installing
    `server` makes a service available; it does not start every server on
    every node.

### The first assignment

| Component | Profiles |
|---|---|
| `mix-shell` (the `mix` binary), `noded` | `base` |
| `compd`, `settingsd`, `portald`, `editd`, `releasesd`, `busviewer`, `ced`, `dopus`, `prefs` | `desktop` |

`server` starts empty: the server programs join it as they move in (mail,
web, blobs and the rest). `releasesd` is a per-user session service and
`editd` serves the session's editors, so both are `desktop`. A headless
mode for either would be its own decision, with suitable supervision,
before it joins `server`.

## Why

- **The two sides share their foundation.** The Bus, noded, Mix, the config
  and props libraries and logging sit under both, and they change almost
  daily. A second repository could pin them as Git dependencies rather than
  wait for releases, but every foundation change would still mean a
  coordinated upgrade on the other side, and consolidating duplicated code
  across the boundary would mean moving it between repositories.
- **Changes cut across both.** The verb registry's move to classes changed
  the registry, its gate and every application in one commit. Across two
  repositories that is coordinated pull requests that can drift apart.
- **The separation that matters can be enforced here.** Headless code
  never needing a GUI stack is a property of a dependency closure, and the
  profile gate checks exactly that for every `base` and `server` component.
  A repository boundary would enforce it less precisely: it says nothing
  about which features or which programs a node gets.
- **This was decided once already.** The
  [source layout decision](2026-10-04-source-layout.md) rejected one
  repository per component so that one dependency graph can be gated,
  shared code consolidated, and changes made atomically. A desktop/server
  split is the same proposal in two pieces, and nothing it relied on has
  changed.
- **What people actually need separated is the build and the install.** A
  mail server should never compile or install the compositor. Profiles say
  that precisely, from data, in one place.

## Alternatives

- **A second repository for server programs.** The strongest case for it:
  an independent lockfile, toolchain and release pipeline, so desktop
  dependency churn never touches a server build and a server fix never
  waits on the desktop. That isolation is real; it loses to the shared,
  fast-moving foundation and the consolidation still to do. A split would
  be the right call if the server side ever needed a different licence,
  private code, its own team or its own release cadence. None of these
  applies. Private deployment detail already lives outside this repository.
- **Cargo features or a second workspace in this repository.** Rejected. A
  second workspace means two lockfiles and two dependency graphs, which is
  what AGENTS.md §0 rules out. Features select code inside a crate, not
  which programs a system gets.
- **A top-level `server/` directory.** Rejected: the top level is
  classified by kind only (AGENTS.md §1). A web server is a service like
  any other; which systems it belongs on is data.

## Consequences

- One `Cargo.lock`: a dependency bump for the desktop also moves the
  servers' resolved versions, and a server fix ships from the same tree as
  that day's desktop work. Each component's tests and the gates catch a
  break; the alternative was version drift between repositories.
- Building a server set compiles only that set's closure (`cargo build -p`),
  so headless builds stay small. A server build host still checks out the
  whole tree, desktop vendor forks included.
- AGENTS.md §2.3 and §2.5 gain the `profiles` field, and §10's checklist
  asks for it.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-one-system-binary/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-one-system-binary.md) -->

# Decision — one system binary

Status: accepted 2026-10-12. Amends [the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md)
(AGENTS.md §2.3, §3.4, §6 and §9).

## The decision

- **One binary, `mix`, carries the shell and every headless daemon.** It is
  built by a new host component, `cli/system` (package `system`, kind `cli`).
  The host's only code is the dispatcher and the global allocator.
- **A daemon is a personality, chosen by the name the binary was started
  as.** `noded`, `maild`, `webd` and the rest are symlinks to `mix` in
  `/opt/mixos/bin`. Each still runs as its own process, under its own unit
  and journal identity, because the kernel names a process after the name it
  was executed by. There are no daemon subcommands under `mix`: the shell's
  first-argument namespace stays the shell's.
  - `mix --personalities` lists what the binary contains, with each
    component's version.
  - An unknown name exits 2 and prints that list.
  - The shell's self re-execution passes `mix` as its name, so a re-exec from
    a daemon personality comes back as the shell.
- **Components keep their identity.** Each daemon keeps its own crate, tests,
  units, metadata, version and verb registry. Its library exports
  `pub fn main() -> ExitCode`; its own `[[bin]]` stays for development
  builds. `cli/mix-shell` becomes a library with no binary.
- **What goes in:** the shell, `noded`, and every headless base and server
  daemon as it arrives, including the headless desktop-profile services.
  **What stays out:** anything with a GUI stack (compd, the applications),
  and any daemon whose dependencies dwarf the rest. The install-profile
  gate's closure check enforces the first.
- **One personality per process.** No setup happens at link or load time.
  The async runtime, TLS provider, signal masks, panic hook and logger are set
  up in the personality's own `main`, never in a shared library's
  initialiser. Each personality passes its own logging identity and records
  its own build provenance. Every personality uses one allocator, mimalloc.
  A test starts every personality and checks its identity.
- **Fleet builds are static.** The shipped binary targets
  `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, fully static, so one file runs on every
  supported distribution regardless of its C library.
- **Shell tests test the shipped binary.** The shell's process-level tests
  live in `cli/system/tests/` and run `mix` as built by the host.

## Why

Every daemon links the same core: the async runtime, serialisation, the Bus,
the Mix evaluator, logging. Linked separately, each carries its own copy, and
every release links that core once per daemon. Measured on the first
two-personality build (the shell and `noded`), the combined binary was 11%
smaller than the two separate ones and its release link took 40% less time.
Both gains grow with each personality. A static musl build cost nothing in
size, startup or evaluator speed, and the same file ran on both
distributions tested.

One file also means one artifact per architecture, one hash to verify and one
version on every node. Running daemons keep the old file's inode, so an
upgrade restarts only the units whose component changed.

Memory is not part of the case: different personalities run different code,
so they share little.

## Consequences

- AGENTS.md §2.3: `cli/system` builds the `mix` binary. `cli/mix-shell` is
  the shell's library and builds no binary.
- AGENTS.md §3.4: a daemon may be installed as a personality, a symlink named
  after its component; units name the symlink.
- AGENTS.md §6: `cli/system` is the one package allowed a non-dev dependency
  on `kind = "cli"` packages.
- AGENTS.md §9: the bootstrap is `cargo build --profile release-fast -p system`.
- Build scripts that built `-p mix-shell` to get `mix` build `-p system`.
- The installer creates each node's personality symlinks from its install
  profiles, keeps the previous binary for rollback, and restarts only changed
  units. The release archive's manifest lists each personality with its
  component version.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-scene-strings/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-scene-strings.md) -->

# Decision — scene strings until Mix reads Fluent

Status: accepted 2026-10-12. Bounds AGENTS.md §4's i18n rule for Mix Scenes content until the gap below is closed.

## The problem

AGENTS.md §4 says user-visible strings come from Fluent catalogues
(`<component>/i18n/<lang>/<component>.ftl`) and that new GUI code does not
hard-code them. Mix Scenes content, the panel, launcher, calendar, notes
and settings scenes in `share/scenes`, is written in Mix, and **Mix has no
Fluent loader**. A scene cannot read a catalogue today. Its strings ("Apps",
the calendar's month names, the launcher's category labels, and the
panel's hover tips) are English literals in Mix.

That is a gap in Mix, not a reason to work around it (AGENTS.md §0).

## The decision

- **Until Mix reads Fluent, a scene library keeps its user-visible strings
  in one table** — the English source — and builds every string through one
  lookup. `share/scenes/lib/models.mix` does this for the panel's hover
  tips: `$TEXT` holds them, `text(key, vars)` fills `{name}` placeholders
  and `counted(n, none, one, many)` chooses the plural form.
- **No new scattered literals.** New user-visible scene strings go into
  such a table, never inline in the model code.
- **The table is the seam.** When Mix gains a Fluent reader, each table
  becomes `share/scenes/i18n/en/<scene-library>.ftl`, keyed exactly as the
  table is, and the lookup reads the session's language with English as
  the fallback. The callers do not change.
- **Older literals** ("Apps" in the panel template, `CATEGORY_LABELS` and
  the month names in `lib/data.mix`) move into tables when their scenes are
  next edited, not as a drive-by.

## Closing the gap

The Mix work is a Fluent reader (parse `.ftl`, resolve a message with
arguments and plural selectors, choose a locale with fallback), added to
`libs/mix` as a builtin or a standard module. This decision is superseded
when that lands and the scene tables are converted.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-screenshot/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-screenshot.md) -->

# Decision — screenshot

Status: accepted 2026-10-12; amended 2026-10-13 (saved shots are named
`YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.png`, as Spectacle can name them, instead of
`Screenshot YYYY-MM-DD HH-MM-SS.png`). Amends
[the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md) (AGENTS.md §3.4).

## The decision

- **The screenshot and annotation app is `apps/screenshot`.** Its package,
  binary and directory are `screenshot`, its app id is
  `dev.mixos.screenshot` and its Bus service and verbs are `screenshot` and
  `screenshot.*`. "Screenshot" is exactly what the app does, and it is the
  word a person looks for in a launcher.
- **It supersedes Cap.** Cap was the iced screenshot app (`apps/cap`,
  `dev.mixos.cap`, verbs `cap.*`) that lived outside this tree. The egui
  port brings its behaviour across under the new name:
  - the engine moves into the `annotation` crate: the immutable capture,
    the editable objects with undo, one painter for preview and export,
    and no-clobber PNG publication;
  - the iced shell is rewritten on the toolkit, with every action a
    registry command.

  Cap's names are retired and stay reserved (§3.5): the binary `cap`, the
  app id `dev.mixos.cap` and the verbs `cap.ping`, `cap.info`,
  `cap.capture`, `cap.cancel`, `cap.open`, `cap.annotate`, `cap.move`,
  `cap.delete`, `cap.crop`, `cap.undo`, `cap.redo`, `cap.export`,
  `cap.show` and `cap.quit`. They are entered in the retired-names
  registry when it lands. None of them was ever registered here.
- **Print Screen starts it.** compd's bindings, in both profiles:
  - Print takes a region;
  - Shift+Print takes the whole output;
  - Alt+Print takes the window that had the keyboard.

  compd launches `screenshot --comp SERVICE --capture MODE`, naming its own
  Bus service (so a nested compd's key captures through that compd) and,
  for a window capture, the window that had the keyboard at the key press.
  There is one window and one headless instance per compositor:
  `screenshot` and `screenshot-headless` for `comp`, `screenshot-<comp>`
  and `screenshot-headless-<comp>` for another when the name fits in 31
  bytes, else `screenshot--<hash>` and `screenshot-headless--<hash>`; a
  window name never starts with `screenshot-headless`. If that window is already running, the new
  process hands the request to it over the Bus (`screenshot.take`) and
  exits. Unsaved annotations are never discarded by a key press: the window
  comes forward and asks first.
- **Saved shots go to the screenshots folder.** Save (Ctrl+S) writes
  `XDG_PICTURES_DIR/Screenshots/YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.png` (local time) with no
  dialog. A taken name gets `_2`, `_3` and so on, and nothing is ever
  replaced. Every save is published on `screenshot.saved` and recorded, so
  an agent gets the latest shots from `screenshot.recent` without being
  told a path.
- **`screenshot` is an accepted name collision.**
  - Arch Linux's `extra/nwg-shell` installs `/usr/bin/screenshot`, a helper
    for that shell. It was the only owner found on 2026-10-12, checked with
    `pacman -F`.
  - In Debian trixie no package installs a `screenshot` in a binary
    directory. The name appears only inside private directories (a GIMP
    plug-in, the Qt examples), checked with the packages.debian.org
    contents search.
  - Fedora was not checked: it has no public file search that works
    without a Fedora host.
  - MixOS installs to `/opt/mixos/bin`, which comes first in its PATH, so a
    MixOS session's `screenshot` is this one. compd launches it from its
    own directory, and the desktop entry names it by absolute path.

## Why

The plain word is the right name for the plain job, and `cap` said
nothing to someone who did not already know it. The collision costs
little: nwg-shell's helper is internal to nwg-shell and is not run by name
inside a MixOS session.

Handing a shot to an agent should need no typing. A fixed folder, a name
that sorts by time, a topic on every save and a query for the latest shots
give the agent the file without the person saying where it is.

## Consequences

- AGENTS.md §3.4 lists the accepted collisions: `mix` (Elixir), `rec` and
  `play` (sox), and `screenshot` (nwg-shell).
- The `screenshot.*` verbs and its drive verbs are registered in
  `docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`.
- compd's binding table gains Print, Shift+Print and Alt+Print. No bare
  F1–F12 key is bound: those belong to the person.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-system-dialogs/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-12-system-dialogs.md) -->

# Decision — shipped system dialogs

Status: accepted 2026-10-12. Widens the scene loader's v1 rule that only
the Scene Editor may be a dialog.

## The problem

The scene host has one dialog seat. A dialog takes it when it loads, keeps
it while loaded, takes the keyboard when it shows and gives it back when it
hides. The loader therefore refused `window.kind: "dialog"` for every
installation except the Scene Editor, so no other part of the desktop could
ask a short question, such as the name for a workspace.

## The decision

- **A system dialog** is a shipped scene template that:
  - is marked `hidden: true` in its shipped `template.conf.mix`;
  - declares `window.kind: "dialog"` in its shipped `scene.mix`;
  - is installed under its own template name.

  The loader allows it to load as a dialog. The permission is read from the
  shipped files under the templates root, never from the user-editable
  installed copy. A shipped dialog that is not hidden, a system dialog
  installed (or forked) under another name, and any other scene edited into
  a dialog are all still refused. The installed copy of a system dialog is
  the person's own, like any installed scene, and keeps the permission its
  name carries.
- **Hidden templates stay out of the gallery**, so people still see one
  dialog scene, the Scene Editor.
- **A system dialog holds the seat only while it shows.** Its owner installs
  it disabled and enables it to ask. The dialog disables itself once its
  dialog is hidden by Save, Cancel or Esc, or by another dialog taking the
  seat.
- **The Scene Editor.** By default the Scene Editor is a native application
  window, not a dialog scene. It never uses the dialog seat, so it and a
  system dialog can both be open. The legacy scene frontend
  (`SCENES_EDITOR_APP=0`) is a dialog scene and keeps priority:
  - opening it pre-empts a system dialog;
  - it holds the seat for as long as it is loaded, hidden or not, so a
    system dialog asked for meanwhile is refused (`DIALOG_BUSY`) and its
    owner says so;
  - unloading it (`scenes.editor.close {unload: true}`) frees the seat.
- **One system dialog at a time.** A dialog asked to show for something else
  while it is already showing (another workspace) refuses until it is saved
  or cancelled. A failed start is rolled back (the scene is disabled again),
  and the dialog releases the seat only when the host's current state shows
  it hidden, never on a stale notice.
- **Focus.** A dialog takes the keyboard when it maps and gives it back when
  it hides. Its `window.autofocus` field gets focus as it opens.

The first system dialog is `share/scenes/workspace-rename`. Right-clicking a
pager button opens it for that workspace, and it names the workspace through
`comp.workspace.rename`.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-13-desk-and-deskd/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-13-desk-and-deskd.md) -->

# Decision — desk and deskd

Status: accepted 2026-10-13. Follows the multi-call precedent of
[rec and play](2026-10-11-rec-and-play.md); within the naming rules of
[the source layout](2026-10-04-source-layout.md) (AGENTS.md §3).

## The decision

- **`desk` is the desktop's applications in one binary.** The GUI apps
  (busviewer, ced, dopus, prefs, screenshot, backdrop, and term when it
  lands) build into one executable, `desk`. Each app's name is a link to
  it in `/opt/mixos/bin`, and the binary runs the app it was started as.
  `desk <app> [args]` does the same, and `desk` alone lists the apps.
- **`deskd` is the desktop's session services in one binary**, by the same
  rule: the services a desktop session runs and a headless host does not
  (portald, settingsd, editd). Each keeps its name as a link and its own
  unit.
- **What stays separate:**
  - `mix` (the shell, on every host);
  - `noded` (the broker, on every host, desktop or not);
  - `hostd` (the host's information and privilege service, on every
    host). It runs as root and is the one way to elevate: it never shares
    a binary with `deskd` or anything else that runs as the session
    account;
  - `compd` (the compositor: its robustness and its dependency set are
    its own).
- **Each app and service is still its own process.** A crash ends one app,
  not the others; units, desktop entries and scripts keep calling
  `/opt/mixos/bin/<name>`.
- **Each crate keeps a `run` entry point and its own `main`**, so
  `cargo run -p ced` and every per-app test work as before. The multi-call
  crates only dispatch. Identity (build info, app ID, version) is passed by
  each app's `run`, never taken from the multi-call crate's package.

## Why

Every egui app links its own egui, wgpu, naga, fonts and icons: about
22 MB of each binary is that shared runtime, and an app's own code is 1 to
3 MB. A measured prototype put six apps (backdrop, busviewer, ced, dopus,
prefs, screenshot; release profile, fat LTO) in one binary: 128.7 MB
separately, 29.4 MB together. Link-time optimisation removes the
duplicates, and running apps share one mapped executable, so the runtime
is in memory once.

Rust dynamic libraries were rejected: there is no stable Rust ABI, libstd
would ship as a shared library, LTO stops at the boundary, and generic code
is still copied into each app. A C-ABI wrapper around egui would be a
second UI API.

## The names

- `desk` and `deskd` are plain nouns, a pair in the `<role>d` convention
  (§3.1, §3.4), unique in the dependency graph, and installed by no Arch
  package (checked 2026-10-13; the other distributions' file lists are
  checked before first use).
- The layers read in order:
  - **MixOS** is the system.
  - **mix** is its shell and language.
  - **noded** is the broker on every host.
  - **hostd** is the host's information and privileged actions, as root,
    on every host.
  - **compd**, **desk** and **deskd** are the desktop.

  A headless host runs `mix`, `noded` and `hostd`; a desktop adds the
  other three.
- A machine running the desktop is "a desk"; numbered instances (a desk
  and its number) are names of machines, not of these binaries.

## Not decided here

When each app and service moves in, the install layout of the links, and
how `component_install.mix` and the unit collector treat a multi-call
binary. Those land with the implementation.

---

<!-- page: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-13-instance-verb-families/ (source: https://mixos.dev/decisions/2026-10-13-instance-verb-families.md) -->

# Instance verb families (schema 3)

Status: accepted, 2026-10-13.

## Context

Some Bus verbs are not one name. A bridge serves one service per instance it
runs, so a verb such as `<instance>.status` exists once for each running
instance, and the instances are known only at runtime. The verb registry
(`docs/spec/bus/verbs.conf.mix`, checked by `tools/verb_registry.mix`) listed
only concrete names, so there was no place to record these verbs or to check
that a name could not be taken by an instance.

## Decision

1. **Schema 3 is additive.** The `verbs` list is unchanged from schema 2, and
   its entries stay concrete in this migration. A new `families` list follows
   it. A family does not stand in for a concrete verb, in the registry or in
   code. This decision does not settle whether a concrete verb may later be
   expressed as a family; that would take its own decision.

2. **Schema 2 takes no families.** A schema 2 file with a `families` key is
   refused, empty or not, so an unvalidated list cannot pass as legacy data.
   Schema 1 stays refused. Schema 3 requires a `families` list, even an empty
   one.

3. **Family fields** are exactly `pattern`, `owner`, `members`, `version`,
   `status`, `class`, in that order, one entry per line, written
   `pattern:"…"` (never `name:"…"`). The fields are validated like the verb
   fields: release versions, the statuses and classes below, and component
   names for the owner.

4. **Pattern.** It is `<app>.<suffix>`, where the literal `<app>` stands for
   the instance name and the suffix is one or more lower identifier segments
   (`call`, `ui.tree`). Catch-all patterns are refused, and each pattern is
   unique across all owners.

5. **Members.** `members` is either `"instances"`, meaning the members are
   runtime instances and are not listed, or a nonempty list of unique Bus
   service names.
   - Families of one owner may share a listed member, so one service can
     implement several families (for example `<app>.call` and `<app>.status`).
   - A listed member used by families of two owners is refused.
   - A listed member may equal the first segment of concrete verbs only when
     every such verb has the family's owner, and the expanded wire name
     (`member.suffix`) is not itself a concrete verb. An exact concrete
     duplicate is always refused.
   - Any other collision is refused, not resolved.

6. **Class semantics** are those of
   `docs/decisions/2026-10-11-verb-classes.md`. A family records its class as
   written; the gate checks that it is one of the four classes and does not
   infer it from the handler.

7. **Family ownership.** A family with `"instances"` belongs to its owner
   component only. The source check accepts an `on @.<suffix>` declaration
   only from the component whose `"instances"` family has that suffix. Every
   such family must be declared at least once in its owner's runtime code.
   Another component declaring the same suffix is refused as a wrong owner.

8. **Declarations come from the native parser.** The source check reads the
   handler metadata of the native `mix lint --json` (lint schema 2). There is
   no fallback reader.

## Checks and their limits

- **Source check (`--source ROOT`).** The gate reads the `.mix` files under
  `apps/`, `services/`, `cli/` and `libs/`. It skips `tests/`, `test/`,
  `benches/`, `fuzz/`, and `*.conf.mix`/`*.spec.mix` files. The declarations
  come from the native parser: each file is passed to `mix lint --json FILE`,
  and every handler whose command starts with `@.` is a declaration. The
  handler metadata is the parsed AST, so nested and duplicate declarations
  count, and text inside quotes, heredocs and comments does not. The source
  is never executed.
  - **Feature detection.** The lint document is schema 2, with a `handlers`
    list. A Mix that answers without it fails with `native Mix lacks parsed
    handler metadata; rebuild current Mix`. There is no fallback parser.
  - **Fail-closed.** A file that does not lint (nonzero exit), output that is
    truncated, a document that is not valid JSON, a wrong `tool`, `files` or
    `summary`, or a handler with a bad `command`, `file` or `line` each make the
    check fail. An unreadable source root or nested source directory fails the
    check too. Diagnostics and source text are never printed.
  - **Walk.** The gate lists each directory with the native `ls` and reads each
    entry with `stat`, recursing by hand. The native `glob` and `walk` skip an
    unreadable directory without an error, so they are not used to prove an
    absence. Test, bench and fuzz directories are skipped before the recursion.
    The source root and each kind directory must be a plain directory (a
    symlink is refused). Trailing slashes are dropped before that check, so a
    symlink named with one is refused too. Only the last component of each such
    path is checked without following links; a symlink in a directory above it
    is followed, as any path is. A symlink anywhere else in a kind's tree is
    refused, and so is a directory that cannot be listed.
  - The check is **structural**. It proves that a handler for the suffix sits
    in the owner's code, not that it registers at runtime. The owner's Bus
    suite tests the runtime registration.
- **Instance check (`--instances DIR`).** Each `*.conf.mix` file stem in DIR
  is checked against the Bus name rule, the reserved names (the `mixos-`
  prefix, `noded` and `noded-*`, the broker's session-name shape), the first
  segments of concrete verbs and the listed family members. A name that is a
  concrete prefix or a listed member is refused whatever its owner. DIR must be
  a plain directory (a trailing slash does not get a symlink past this), and an
  unreadable DIR fails the check. Any path may hold glob characters, since `ls`
  takes a name, not a pattern. Configs are flat by design: the gate lists the
  top level only, dot files included. A `*.conf.mix` entry in a subdirectory,
  and any other file, is ignored; none of them is a runtime config, and the gate
  neither recurses into them nor reads their contents. Symlinks, directories and other non-regular files named
  `*.conf.mix` are refused, and so are configs when the registry has no
  instances family. Config contents and tokens are never read.
- **Offline.** Neither check touches the network or a running broker. A name
  that passes here is a name the Bus will accept, as far as the Bus's own
  rules go. A runtime refusal (for example, a broker that has already
  registered the name) is still possible and is not this gate's concern.
- **Mesh exposure is unchanged.** Nothing in the gate or the registry changes
  what any mesh peer can reach. The families describe names; a service's own
  configuration decides what it serves.

## Consequences

- Schema 2 files stay valid as long as they carry no families.
- The source check needs a Mix whose `mix lint --json` reports handler
  metadata (lint schema 2). An older Mix fails the source check until it is
  rebuilt; the gate does not fall back to another reader.
- A new instance family needs a family entry, and an `on @.<suffix>` handler
  in its owner's code, in the same change.
- Public examples use only the neutral fixture names `fakeapp`, `demod` and
  `otherd`. No runtime instance name belongs in this repository's docs.

---
